texto_fonte:
The European Union now requires AI-generated text to be watermarked so that it can be identified as such. But tests on OpenAI’s new textGrain watermark, released in October and developed to comply with the new EU law, show that these watermarks often do not survive additional editing of the text or when it’s under 150 words. With no clear legal benchmark for how well watermarks should work, it’s uncertain whether textGrain will meet Europe’s transparency rules, which could cost the company significantly and make it difficult to detect AI-generated text as models grow more sophisticated.
AI models calculate the probabilities of different possible next tokens (the next word or word fragment it generates) based on the text already written, then select one and repeat that process until the response is complete. After the prompt “today the weather is…,” for example, says Xiang Li, co-author of the textGrain technical report and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pennsylvania, the model might weigh “warm” or “cool” as possible next words.
A watermark uses a secret key to generate pseudorandom values: numbers produced by a mathematical process, which influence which token the model suggests. This creates a statistical pattern in the text that a detector with the same secret key can look for, Li says.
What makes textGrain different from other watermarks is that it uses entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a model’s word choices are, as a resource that can be budgeted when embedding a watermark. Developers specify how much entropy or unpredictability they want to allow, and textGrain adjusts to that target.
This gives developers more control over the balance between embedding a detectable signal and preserving variation in the model’s output, Li says. “We can think of entropy as a resource, a kind of money. […] In our approach, we can accurately determine how much of that resource we want to consume.”
Limits of AI Watermark Detection
The watermark is invisible to readers. But a positive result does not show how much a person contributed to a passage, and a negative result does not prove that a text was human-written.
OpenAI’s false-positive rate is 1 percent, meaning the detector is designed to wrongly flag about one in 100 unwatermarked passages. In tests on psychology questions from the ELI5 database, which gathers questions and answers from the /r/explainlikeimfive subreddit, the model detected watermarks in about 80 percent of 200-token text (approximately 150 words) compared to 95 percent of 400-token text (approximately 300 words).
Li says this is a “basic limitation” of text watermarking technologies and would be complicated to solve. Short passages may not contain enough watermark evidence for reliable detection, even with additional computation, he adds, while longer passages generally provide more.
Editing also weakens the signal. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing just 10 percent of words with synonyms reduced detection from 92 percent to 66 percent; replacing up to 25 percent cut the detection rate to 17 percent, according to OpenAI. Because the watermark depends on preceding tokens, changing one word can disrupt the signal at several positions, Li says.
OpenAI says watermarking alone is not enough to determine whether content is AI-generated.
TextGrain will “complement” other provenance tools, such as content credentials in the metadata and SynthID watermarks developed by Google DeepMind for images and audio outputs. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.
EU AI Act Transparency Obligations
The transparency obligations in Article 50 of the EU AI Act went into effect on 2 August. The law requires providers of systems generating synthetic audio, images, video, or text to mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Technical solutions must be “effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible,” according to the law.
The EU’s Code of Practice offers a voluntary way for providers to show how they will be compliant. This code does not require watermarks on outputs shorter than 200 tokens.
Thomas Souverain, a postdoctoral fellow on AI Ethics at the Institute of Advanced Education in Paris, says the legislation is open to interpretation.
Souverain says that the early methodology behind textGrain seems reliable and could work better than its competitors at identifying AI-generated text. OpenAI says textGrain matched or outperformed Google’s SynthID Text in its own tests, but those results have not been independently verified. Until independent researchers can test it, and while the AI Act’s criteria still lack measurable thresholds, it is too early to say whether textGrain meets legal requirements.
“We only have a technical study … there hasn’t been a peer-reviewed academic article, and we don’t [yet] have access to a precise protocol [for textGrain],” Souverain says.
OpenAI is working with a limited group of researchers that includes John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, and researchers at the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies in Bratislava, Slovakia.
Thickstun and Dominik Macko, a senior researcher at KInIT, says they had only just gained access and had not yet begun evaluating the system. Macko says his team plans to test textGrain’s “robustness” across different subject areas, languages, and text lengths.
If textGrain is eventually found to not meet the EU’s requirements, Souverain says OpenAI could face a fine of up to 7 percent of its annual income.
Souverain also calls on OpenAI to make textGrain open-source so that researchers not on their team can “identify all the faults, paraphrases and possible translation faults” of the model by trying to break it.
“I see the corporate interest, if there is a big flaw detected, a big weakness, [that] it is detected in the background,” he said. “But I would like to see an even more open phase, such as today with SynthID, [where] we have access to the methods.”

texto_fonte:
Model shows factories and employees can profit from idle car batteries at work
Researchers from Skoltech—a VEB.RF Group institution—have developed an optimization framework to help factories compare strategies for using onsite solar power and the electric vehicles of employees to reduce electricity costs. Evaluated in a Moscow case study, the approach accounts for industrial electricity billing rules, operating decisions and drivers' willingness to participate, helping businesses assess options before investing.
The study was published in Applied Energy.
As the share of renewables in the global electricity mix is projected to keep growing, finding enough land for solar and wind farms and other generation facilities is becoming increasingly difficult. This challenge is compounded by the need for infrastructure upgrades where existing transmission lines cannot carry the additional output.
Generating electricity close to where it is consumed could provide part of the solution by cutting the need for long-distance transmission and making use of existing buildings or developed sites. Factories are prime candidates: Their large electricity demand can absorb on-site generation, and their roofs and industrial grounds mitigate the need for new land.
Businesses considering this route need to work out how to combine available resources into a financially worthwhile project. Cars parked at work sit idle for hours.
With bidirectional chargers, which allow electricity to flow into and out of car batteries, employees' electric vehicles could supply part of a factory's needs. Known as vehicle-to-grid technology, this approach can add flexibility to a factory's energy use. Unlike stationary storage, however, cars arrive and leave with their owners, who need enough charge at the end of the day for making their trips and who may opt out entirely.
Factory owners can manage when cars charge and whether participating vehicles may supply power back to the workplace. Each arrangement involves different operating decisions and financial considerations. Add solar generation into the mix, and the picture changes further.
For a case study, the researchers looked at the Russian market, where industrial consumers pay for electricity at hourly prices and for capacity linked to demand during particular peak hours. Solar generation and flexible vehicle charging can therefore reduce different parts of the electricity bill.
The Skoltech team identified a lack of long-term investment assessments that would account for solar power, workplace vehicle-to-grid supply, driver participation and Russian billing rules. The framework proposed in the study links driver participation, charging prices, compensation for supplying electricity and car battery charge levels. This means that the incentives offered determine how much flexibility is available: Not every connected car is automatically counted as available.
For a test period of 10 years, the researchers compared six supply scenarios: grid-only supply, solar panels alone, vehicle-to-grid alone, solar with managed charging, and combined solar and vehicle-to-grid under fixed and behavioral participation assumptions.
Under an unchanging vehicle fleet and solar infrastructure, the model jointly optimized operating schedules, charging prices and driver compensation within battery and connectivity limits, then assessed the resulting financial returns.
Distinct economic opportunities emerged depending on the scenario: While solar generation reduced electricity purchases, coordinating vehicle charging and discharging created additional value under the case-study conditions. Managed charging provided benefits without requiring battery discharge, and bidirectional operation offered further flexibility.
Accounting for driver participation produced more conservative financial estimates than assuming every technically available car participates. In terms of capital efficiency, vehicle-to-grid solutions alone are expected to recoup their investment faster than when paired with solar cells, even though the latter approach yields greater long-term returns.
"Employees' electric cars create an opportunity to use the same battery for personal transport and workplace energy flexibility. We factor drivers' willingness to participate into the coordination of solar power, charging and discharging. This helps businesses compare operating arrangements and assess whether the additional flexibility justifies the investment," said the study's lead author, Ahmed Eltwam, a Ph.D. student in Skoltech's Engineering Systems program.
"A systematic assessment of project viability could encourage more investment in onsite solar power and workplace vehicle-to-grid services. Businesses could lower electricity costs, and employees could be paid for the flexibility their vehicles provide. At a broader scale, deployment coordinated with grid needs could support national renewable energy targets while avoiding some of the costly network upgrades," said the study's principal investigator, associate professor of the practice Marina Dolmatova of Skoltech Energy.
The findings are based on simulations with estimated market and operating inputs. Participation assumptions were informed by published research rather than a workplace survey. Although evaluated for Moscow, the framework can be adapted to local electricity prices, billing rules, demand, weather and vehicle availability.
Financial outcomes remain specific to the analyzed conditions, including the alignment of operation with capacity-charge hours. Testing and calibrating the model against real workplace charging behavior and operating data is a priority for future research.
More information

candidato.titulo: Vazamentos do Smart Sampa expõem fragilidades de sistema de monitoramento
candidato.resumo: Raquel Rolnik aponta riscos à privacidade, discriminação pelo reconhecimento facial e falhas de segurança digital

texto_fonte:
O segundo vazamento de dados sigilosos do Smart Sampa, sistema de monitoramento da Prefeitura de São Paulo, reacende o debate sobre a segurança e a confiabilidade do programa. Segundo denúncia do Portal Uol, cerca de 17 mil câmeras tiveram informações expostas. Para a professora Raquel Rolnik, o episódio revela uma contradição: um sistema criado para ampliar a segurança acaba produzindo o efeito oposto, ao expor dados e imagens de ambientes públicos.
Entre os casos mais graves estão imagens captadas dentro de Centros de Atenção Psicossocial (Caps), creches e Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBSs), o que representa uma séria violação de privacidade. A professora lembra que o Smart Sampa já era alvo de questionamentos desde a licitação, especialmente pelos riscos de discriminação associados ao reconhecimento facial. Especialistas e parlamentares alertaram, na época, para o chamado racismo algorítmico, já que a tecnologia apresenta maior índice de erros na identificação de pessoas negras.
Outro ponto de preocupação era a previsão de alertas automáticos baseados em critérios como vadiagem, permanência, mendicância e cor, que poderiam reforçar a discriminação contra a população em situação de rua. Somados aos elevados custos, à invasão de privacidade e às vulnerabilidades de segurança digital, os episódios de vazamento reforçam, segundo Rolnik, a necessidade de interromper imediatamente o sistema e submetê-lo a uma revisão.
